name: Uber
summary: Uber's careers site describes a talent-team conversation, a chat with the hiring manager, a technical interview for tech roles, a job-related exercise for some roles, and a team interview. Candidates commonly report design questions built around real-time, location-based systems, and Uber says how you approach a problem matters as much as the solution.
rounds: Onsite loop: coding, system design and a collaboration / behavioral interview

questions.text: How would you design the matching of riders to drivers in a busy city?
covers: What 'best match' means: pickup time, fairness to drivers, overall wait times
Finding nearby drivers fast with a geographic index, updated as drivers move
Handling peaks, drivers who decline, and two riders matched to one driver

questions.text: Tell me about a time you owned a problem outside your role.
covers: The problem and why nobody else was fixing it
What you did, including who you brought in
The result and whether it stayed fixed

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to make a trade-off between speed and quality.
covers: The deadline and the quality risk
How you chose, and what you did to limit the downside
What happened, and what you'd choose next time

questions.text: Tell me about a time you used data to change someone's mind.
covers: Their view and why it was reasonable
The data you gathered and how you checked it
How you presented it and what changed

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked with operations, support or another non-engineering team to fix a customer problem.
covers: The customer problem and what each team could see of it
How you worked together and kept everyone informed
The fix and how you knew customers were better off

questions.text: Tell me about a launch that didn't go as planned. What did you change afterwards?
covers: What went wrong and how quickly it was caught
Your part in the response
The process change that followed

questions.text: How would you estimate a trip's arrival time, and how would you make the estimate better over time?
covers: Routing on the road map with live and historical traffic
Learning from past trips: time of day, weather, pickup delays
Measuring error against actual arrival times and improving the worst cases

questions.text: How would you design the live map that shows a rider where their driver is?
covers: How often the driver's app sends location, balancing accuracy with battery and data
Pushing updates to the rider over a persistent connection
Smoothing GPS jumps and handling dropped connections

questions.text: How would you design a food-delivery order flow so the restaurant, courier and customer all see the same status?
covers: An order state machine with clear allowed transitions
Events published to each party, with retries and duplicate handling
What happens when a step fails: a restaurant doesn't confirm, a courier cancels

questions.text: How would you store drivers' locations so you can quickly find the nearest available ones?
covers: A spatial index, such as geohashes, a quadtree or hexagonal cells
Frequent updates kept in memory, partitioned by region
Filtering by availability and vehicle type, and expanding the search when none are close

questions.text: Rider cancellations rose in one city last week. How would you find out why?
covers: Checking the data first: a tracking change, a holiday, an app release
Breaking it down by time, area, wait time, rider versus driver cancellations
The most likely cause and how you'd confirm it

questions.text: Why Uber, and which part of the business interests you most?
covers: A specific area, such as mobility, delivery or freight, and why
A link to your skills or experience
The problem there you'd most like to work on

questions.text: Which Uber product would you improve for riders, drivers or merchants, and how would you measure the result?
covers: One user group and a specific pain point
The change and the trade-off it brings for the other sides of the marketplace
A success metric and a guardrail

tips: Real-time, location-based systems are favourite design topics.
Uber's hiring page suggests reading its newsroom for recent launches and priorities; mention one that connects to the team.
In design rounds, talk about failure: lost connections, GPS errors, retries and duplicate requests.
Prepare stories with numbers for the hiring manager chat, which goes deeper into your skills and decisions.
For some roles, expect a job-related exercise; if you present it in the team interview, explain your choices, not just the results.
